chunks: And upon you be peace, and the mercy of Allah and His blessings, now to proceed:

Know that in front of you lies an impassable valley wherein the light-burdened man will be in a better condition than the heavy-burden one, and the slow-paced would be in a worse condition than the swift-paced. Your terminating point at the other end of this passage will necessarily be either Paradise or Hell. Therefore, investigate for yourself before alighting, and prepare the place before getting down, because after death there can be no preparation nor return to this world.

key_terms.الْمُثْقِلُ: the one who carries a heavy burden (of sins/deeds)
key_terms.الْمُخِفُّ: the one who carries a light burden (of sins/deeds)
key_terms.مُسْتَعْتَبٌ: one who is given a chance to make amends

ai.seo_question: What is the significance of preparing for death in Nahj al-Balagha?
ai.summary: Delivered during the pivotal post-Siffin period, this advice underscores the urgency of spiritual preparation amidst political turmoil, framing life as a steep, inevitable ascent where haste or hesitation in piety dictates one's eternal destination. It highlights the Shia concept of *hazir al-mawt* (being mindful of death) as a proactive strategy to secure a favorable 'landing' in the afterlife before the finality of death precludes any opportunity for repentance or return.
